title: Measuring SAE Feature Sensitivity Decay Across Distribution Shifts

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: characterizing SAE feature sensitivity is a prerequisite for trusting SAE-based safety audits, but it is more of a methodological contribution than a direct safety improvement. The chain to safety requires that SAEs eventually be used for safety monitoring.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Using SAELens to load pre-trained SAEs, collecting top activating examples, generating template-based paraphrases, and measuring activation fractions is accessible work. Primarily data collection and measurement with well-documented tools.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: sample 200 features, collect top 5 examples each, generate paraphrases via templates, measure activation fraction, compare across layers/frequency/width. Systematic measurement with clear deliverable (sensitivity score distribution).

novelty.reasoning: This idea is directly addressed by 'Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity' (arXiv:2509.23717, OpenReview 2025). That paper introduces a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity — how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples — using LM-generated paraphrases. Key findings include: many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width, and sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality distinct from interpretability. The proposed methodology (sample 200 features, collect top activating examples, generate paraphrases, measure activation fraction, compare across layers/frequency/width) is almost exactly the methodology of the published paper.
